questions.prompt: The word “Yet” at the beginning of the second sentence signals
questions.explanation: “Yet” introduces a contrast between preserving data and the insufficiency of storage alone.

support.summary: Yet, however and nevertheless commonly mark contrast.
support.example: “We stored everything. Yet we still could not trust the data.”
support.trap: Do not confuse “yet” as a contrast marker with its use in expressions such as “not yet”.

stimuli.label: Text 2
stimuli.text: Organizations often create a data lake because they want to preserve raw information for future use. Yet storage alone does not create analytical value. If datasets have no ownership, catalog, lineage, or quality rules, the lake may become easier to fill than to trust. Governance is therefore not the opposite of flexibility; it is what makes flexibility sustainable.
stimuli.source: Original passage written for this simulation.

questions.prompt: Which situation best illustrates the risk described in Text 2?
options: An analyst rejects a dataset because a quality rule detects an error.
A database has a documented schema and quality checks.
A catalog records dataset lineage and ownership.
A team stores raw files while also maintaining governance metadata.
A lake contains many datasets, but analysts cannot identify their origin or responsible owner.
questions.explanation: The passage warns about lakes that are easy to fill but difficult to trust because ownership, catalog, lineage and quality rules are absent.
optionExplanations: A rule detecting an error demonstrates governance working.
This is governance, not the risk.
The text does not oppose raw storage when governance exists.

support.summary: Translate the abstract risk into a concrete scenario.
support.example: Questions such as 'Who owns this file?' and 'Where did it come from?' are governance questions.
support.trap: A realistic distractor often contains the same technology but with the missing control restored.

questions.prompt: In “it is what makes flexibility sustainable”, the word “what” introduces
options: a nominal clause meaning 'the thing that'.
questions.explanation: “What makes flexibility sustainable” functions as a noun phrase: the thing that makes flexibility sustainable.
optionExplanations: It is not an interrogative use here.
The construction is active: governance makes flexibility sustainable.

support.summary: In this use, “what” is close to “the thing that”.
support.example: “Data quality is what makes the report credible.”
support.trap: Portuguese speakers may read “what” only as an interrogative form and miss its nominal-clause function.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is closest in meaning to the last sentence of Text 2?
options: Flexibility is sustainable only when governance is absent.
Governance is useful only after flexibility has failed.
Governance and flexibility can be complementary.
questions.explanation: The author rejects a false opposition and presents governance as a condition that sustains flexibility.
optionExplanations: The text treats governance as part of sustainable operation, not a late remedy only.

support.summary: Preserve the logical relation, not just shared vocabulary.
support.example: “Not the opposite; it sustains it” implies complementarity.
support.trap: FGV often uses an option with the same nouns but a reversed relation.

questions.prompt: Considere a afirmação: “Se um conjunto de dados está normalizado, então não possui dependências parciais incompatíveis com a 2FN.” A inexistência dessas dependências é, em relação à normalização mencionada, uma condição
options: necessária, mas não apresentada como suficiente.
equivalente apenas quando a chave é simples.
questions.explanation: Na proposição P→Q, Q é condição necessária para P; a frase não autoriza concluir Q→P.
optionExplanations: Q é consequência necessária segundo a afirmação.
A estrutura lógica dada não depende dessa restrição adicional.

support.summary: Em P→Q: P é suficiente para Q; Q é necessária para P.
support.example: “Se chove, a rua molha” não permite concluir que rua molhada implica chuva.
support.trap: A FGV explora a inversão entre linguagem cotidiana e estrutura formal.
